source.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
source.authors: Xin-Yu Zhou; De-Long Chen; Samuel Cahyawijaya; Xu-Feng Duan; Zhen-Guang G. Cai

record.tranche_reason: Measures agreement between models and finds that it varies across language datasets and is associated with models’ training-language exposure, refining the scope of cross-model convergence.
record.gate_note: The paper measures mutual-k-nearest-neighbor agreement across models’ linguistic-similarity structures, reporting aggregate scores by language dataset. It does not test whether alignment rises with model size or capability. Results on linguistic categories, semantic similarity, and cross-language phenomena do not measure the claim’s cross-model convergence behavior and are not rows here.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Platonic paper's mutual-k-NN alignment metric to 104 LLMs of different architectures, data and sizes, in a new setting: similarity structures of activation differences on minimal pairs. It reports how alignment changes across input datasets (English, Chinese, Russian) and how it groups by training language. This bears on V6 (input dependence) and V7 (incomplete, data-linked alignment). It does not frame itself as refuting the claim, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors say cross-LLM consistency of linguistic similarity is 'strongly influenced' by pretraining data, with higher agreement in higher-resource languages, and they link the Chinese clustering to pretraining language. The paper's other conclusions concern linguistic categories, semantic similarity and cross-lingual structure, which do not bear on convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the mutual-k-nearest-neighbors alignment metric attributed to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but applies it to linguistic-similarity structures derived from minimal pairs and compares language datasets rather than testing alignment growth with scale or capability.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment differs across the English, Chinese, and Russian datasets; the Chinese UMAP shows clustering by models’ training-language group.
record.problems: The analysis samples 10% of each dataset for alignment scoring. It reports no uncertainty estimates or control comparisons. The association between language exposure and alignment is not causally isolated.

untested.parts: The 104 models span sizes, but alignment is never analysed against size or capability.
No vision models and no image-caption pairs.
No comparison of seeds within one architecture.
No mapping, stitching or interchangeability test.
No test of recurring neurons, SAE features or circuits.
Only one metric and one k setting (1% of the pool); similarity is cosine only, and there is no layer-wise breakdown of alignment. Only input language/dataset is varied.
No test of a plateau with scale and no causal manipulation of training data or objectives.

missing.what: The paper states that models from the same family (same creator, different sizes, or base/chat versions) cluster together in the alignment UMAP. This is evidence that shared training data or recipe drives alignment.
Alignment-score distributions are unimodal for English and Russian but bimodal for Chinese. This is part of the input-dependence picture.

record.verdict_notes: What is compared across models is the neighbour structure of activation-difference vectors from five sampled layers; it is unclear how the layers are combined for the alignment score. No uncertainty is reported. The language effect is confounded with dataset differences (number of phenomena, sample size, k). The study is not an original source, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: No test of whether alignment rises with model size or capability.
No alignment test between vision and language models on paired images and captions.
No comparison of same-architecture models trained from different seeds or of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Tests differences across English, Chinese, and Russian datasets, but not alternative similarity metrics, different k settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Reports incomplete and training-language-associated alignment, but does not test for a plateau or causally isolate shared training data or objectives from other model differences.

rows.subject: 104 LLMs (aggregate pairwise alignment)
rows.operation_detail: Computed pairwise mutual-k-nearest-neighbor alignment scores between LLMs’ linguistic-similarity structures.
rows.note: The score is an aggregate over pairwise alignment among the 104 LLMs; the paper describes it as 47.1% overlap of top-1% similar minimal pairs on average.
rows.check: For V7, an average of 0.471 on English is clearly incomplete alignment, which is what V7 says; mark it observed, not partial. For V6 the row only counts as a contrast point together with R2 and R3. No chance baseline is stated; with k at 1% of the pool, chance overlap is about 0.01. Datasets also differ in sample size and k, which confounds the contrast.

rows.subject: 104 LLMs (aggregate pairwise alignment)
rows.operation_detail: Computed pairwise mutual-k-nearest-neighbor alignment scores between LLMs’ linguistic-similarity structures.
rows.note: The score is an aggregate over pairwise alignment among the 104 LLMs; the paper describes it as 41.4% overlap of top-1% similar minimal pairs on average.
rows.check: 0.414 on Chinese is incomplete alignment and lower than English; observed for V7. The distribution is bimodal, per the paper. Baseline not stated; dataset, phenomena set and k all differ from R1.

rows.subject: 104 LLMs (aggregate pairwise alignment)
rows.operation_detail: Computed pairwise mutual-k-nearest-neighbor alignment scores between LLMs’ linguistic-similarity structures.
rows.note: The score is an aggregate over pairwise alignment among the 104 LLMs; the paper describes it as 13.9% overlap of top-1% similar minimal pairs on average.
rows.check: Alignment falls to 0.139 on Russian, a lower-resource language for most models. That is the weakening under other inputs that V6 describes, so mark it observed. It remains well above chance (about 0.01), so the weakening is substantial but not a vanishing.

rows.subject: 104 LLMs (aggregate pairwise alignment)
rows.operation_detail: Visualized model relationships using UMAP based on pairwise alignment scores.
rows.measure: Clustering of model alignment scores by training-language group
rows.value: Two distinct clusters: one predominantly bilingual and multilingual models, the other primarily English-only models.
rows.note: The authors interpret this clustering as evidence that alignment scores correlate with models’ pretraining language.
rows.check: The Chinese clustering by training language (bilingual/multilingual vs English-only) bears on V7's training-data explanation. It is a UMAP pattern with no statistic, and the language groups also differ in model family and creator. Its link to V6 is weak: it shows model grouping, not dependence on inputs, so drop V6.

relationships.condition: Mutual-k-NN alignment among 104 LLMs on BLiMP (English), SLING (Chinese) and RuBLiMP (Russian)
relationships.reason: Average alignment falls from 0.471 (R1) to 0.414 (R2) to 0.139 (R3) as the input language changes. Datasets also differ in phenomena and sample size.
relationships.display_finding: Average alignment fell from 0.471 on English to 0.414 on Chinese and 0.139 on Russian benchmarks, which also differed in tested phenomena and sample size.

relationships.condition: Same 104 LLMs; all three datasets, plus the Chinese-data clustering
relationships.reason: Alignment stays far from complete (0.14–0.47; R1–R3). On Chinese, models group by training language (R4), consistent with a shared-data explanation. This is correlational, with no causal isolation.
relationships.display_finding: Alignment ranged from 0.14 to 0.47, and Chinese comparisons grouped models by training language, suggesting an association with shared training data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BLiMP English, SLING Chinese, and RuBLiMP Russian
reader_labels.reason: Aggregate alignment differs across the three input datasets (R1–R3), with the paper reporting lower agreement for Russian than for English or Chinese.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Across the three language datasets and the Chinese-dataset model clustering
reader_labels.reason: Alignment scores are incomplete and vary by dataset (R1–R3); on Chinese data, model groupings also correlate with training-language exposure (R4). The study reports an association, not a causal isolation of shared training data.
